analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and senior staff from trading individual stocks and from corporate board seats.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban individual stock trading by members of Congress was referred to three House committees and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar sitting members of Congress and senior congressional employees from buying or selling individual stocks, commodities, futures, or similar investments, from taking net short positions, and from serving on for-profit corporate boards. Members could keep investments they held before taking office, divest within six months, or place them in an approved blind trust. Knowing violations would carry a civil penalty of at least 10% of the value of the trade [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: The public, which would gain clearer assurance that lawmakers cannot profit personally from information and decisions acquired in office. Members themselves would benefit from a clearer, uniform rule replacing the current disclosure-only regime, which requires reporting trades but allows them.

how_it_helps.text: Bars members and covered congressional staff from buying or selling individual securities, commodities, futures, or comparable derivatives.
Prohibits net short positions, closing a way to bet against companies the government may regulate or rescue.
Bans members from serving as officers or board members of for-profit corporations.
Attaches a civil penalty of at least 10% of the value of the violating trade to knowing violations.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and covered senior staff, who would have to divest individual holdings, move them into blind trusts, give up corporate board seats, and risk civil penalties of at least 10% of the value of a violating trade.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and senior staff

drawbacks.text: The ban reaches beyond members to senior congressional staff, who would have to divest individual stocks within six months or rely on blind trusts, a real burden for some.

Enforcement runs through the House and Senate Ethics committees themselves, and the civil penalty applies only to knowing violations, so critics could fairly argue the law would be as weakly enforced as the STOCK Act's disclosure rules have been.
Exceptions allow members to keep investments held before taking office and rely on approved blind trusts, which rely on trustee independence rather than outright divestment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is closing a loophole that lets lawmakers profit from information gathered in office; the cost is minor for members (divesting into diversified funds or blind trusts, penalty exposure) and no meaningful public downside. The main weakness is enforcement: the Ethics committees administer it and penalties apply only to knowing violations, so teeth depend on those committees. Its only concrete effect was to die in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and its sponsor never brought it to the floor, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 26, 2020 and referred the same day to the Financial Services, Agriculture, and House Administration committees.
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote; the record ends at the referrals.
It drew 9 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican cosponsors, and no companion action is shown in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress keep the right to trade individual stocks while holding legislative power over the companies they trade. No one else is better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress who trade stocks

for.name: Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House leadership and committee chairs
against.role: Controlled the House agenda and committee calendars
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or a floor vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsors are listed; the bill never got far enough for a vote to reveal the parties' actual positions.

industries.industry: Sitting members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: They would lose the ability to trade individual securities and hold corporate board seats, and face civil penalties for knowing violations. The interest that stopped the bill was their own.

Members' individual trading accounts generate commissions and managed-asset relationships; the bill would end those accounts for a few hundred well-connected clients. Impact is small but directionally negative.
